title: Lamentations 3:34–47
context: The afflicted man, still speaking in the manner of wisdom teaching, says the Lord does not approve crushing prisoners, denying a man his right before the Most High, or subverting a man in his cause (3:34–36). He then asks who can speak and see it come to pass unless the Lord commands it, whether evil and good do not come from the mouth of the Most High (3:37–38), and why a living man should complain when punished for his sins (3:39). Here “evil” most naturally means calamity, the disaster the city has suffered, set beside good (compare Isaiah 45:7; Amos 3:6; Job 2:10), though readers weigh how far the line reaches. Both traditions affirm the LORD’s rule over calamity and both deny that God is the author of sin; their difference over how God relates to evil carried out by human agents, here Babylon, is treated at Judges 9:23 and is not restated. In 3:40 the voice turns to “us”: the community calls itself to search its ways and return to the LORD, to lift heart and hands to God in the heavens (3:41), and then prays a confession and complaint, “We have transgressed and have rebelled. You have not pardoned” (3:42), followed by anger, a cloud that blocks prayer, shame among the peoples, mocking enemies, terror, and the pit (3:43–47). Confession, wrath, and the plea for mercy are shared ground here, and the prayer’s unresolved ending is left standing as the poem leaves it.

verses.text: To crush under foot all the prisoners of the earth,
verses.arminianNotes: Verses 34–36 form one sentence that ends “the Lord doesn’t approve,” and crushing “all the prisoners of the earth” under foot is the first wrong named. Arminian readers see God’s moral concern for the oppressed, which stands even while he judges his own people through foreign armies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Lord’s disapproval of oppression as a reflection of his holy justice, which holds every oppressor to account even when he uses them as instruments (compare Isaiah 10:5–12). Shared ground: both traditions hear God’s care for prisoners and his opposition to cruelty, including Babylon’s.

verses.text: to turn away the right of a man before the face of the Most High,
verses.arminianNotes: The second wrong is “to turn away the right of a man before the face of the Most High,” perverting justice in God’s presence, perhaps in a court where judgment should reflect his own. Arminian readers emphasize that God sees all injustice and holds the guilty responsible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the Most High is the judge before whom every human court stands, so denying a person’s right is an offense against him directly. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as a statement of God’s justice and as encouragement that wrongs done to the afflicted are not unseen.

verses.text: to subvert a man in his cause, the Lord doesn’t approve.
verses.arminianNotes: “To subvert a man in his cause, the Lord doesn’t approve.” Arminian readers see the end of the sentence as a clear moral boundary: God never approves injustice, and this assurance helps the sufferer distinguish God’s just judgment from the cruelty of human agents.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that God never approves injustice even when he governs events that include it, and they read the line as guarding against any idea that God is the author of human wickedness. Shared ground: both traditions take 3:34–36 as the moral frame for the harder lines that follow in 3:37–38.

verses.text: Who is he who says, and it comes to pass, when the Lord doesn’t command it?
verses.arminianNotes: “Who is he who says, and it comes to pass, when the Lord doesn’t command it?” Arminian readers affirm God’s sovereignty over events and hear the question as a rebuke to human boasting, while understanding God’s rule to include permitting free agents to act within his purposes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the question as a strong statement of God’s decree: nothing comes to pass apart from his command, which includes his governance of human plans. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that history is not outside God’s rule; their difference on how God relates to evil done by human agents is treated at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: Doesn’t evil and good come out of the mouth of the Most High?
verses.arminianNotes: “Doesn’t evil and good come out of the mouth of the Most High?” Arminian readers take “evil” here as calamity, the disaster of judgment set beside blessing (compare Isaiah 45:7; Amos 3:6; Job 2:10), and they read the line as God’s sovereignty over judgment, not his authorship of sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read “evil” here chiefly as calamity decreed by God in just judgment, and they affirm that God governs all things while remaining holy and free from the guilt of sin. Shared ground: neither tradition makes God the author of sin; their difference over permitting and directing versus ordaining and governing evil done by human agents is treated at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: Why should a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?
verses.arminianNotes: “Why should a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?” Arminian readers hear a call to accept just discipline without bitter murmuring, and they note that being still alive is itself a mercy that leaves room to turn back to God (3:40).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as directing the sufferer away from accusing God and toward confession, since judgment for sin is deserved and life itself is grace. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as a word against bitter complaint, not against lament, which the poem itself models throughout.

verses.text: Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The voice shifts to the community: “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.” Arminian readers stress the call to repentance as a genuine invitation the people can heed by grace, and they see the plural voice drawing the whole city into confession.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers welcome the same call and add that turning to the LORD is itself the fruit of his grace (compare 5:21, where the community asks the LORD to turn them). Shared ground: both traditions read 3:40 as a real summons to self-examination and repentance, and both see in it the way through judgment.

verses.text: Let’s lift up our heart with our hands to God in the heavens.
verses.arminianNotes: “Let’s lift up our heart with our hands to God in the heavens.” Arminian readers hear a call to sincere prayer in which outward gesture and inward heart agree, and they see it as the community’s responsive turn toward the God who invites them to return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same summons to wholehearted prayer, with lifted hands empty of merit that look only to God in the heavens for mercy. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as the bridge from self-examination to confession, and both warn against outward religion without the heart (compare Joel 2:13).

verses.text: “We have transgressed and have rebelled. You have not pardoned.
verses.arminianNotes: The community confesses: “We have transgressed and have rebelled. You have not pardoned.” Arminian readers see honest confession as necessary and note that the people do not yet sense forgiveness, so confession and complaint stand together without a forced resolution.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the confession as a true acknowledgment of guilt and the complaint as faith struggling with God’s apparent silence, not as a denial of his mercy. Shared ground: both traditions read “You have not pardoned” as the felt experience of ongoing judgment, not a final statement about forgiveness.

verses.text: “You have covered us with anger and pursued us. You have killed. You have not pitied.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have covered us with anger and pursued us. You have killed. You have not pitied.” Arminian readers hear the community naming the full weight of judgment, and they see in such honesty a faith that refuses to look away from what has happened while still praying.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s anger as his just response to covenant rebellion, and they note that the community addresses it to God, showing that they still look to him alone. Shared ground: both traditions read these strong words soberly, as the grief of a city that has seen death, and neither softens them.

verses.text: You have covered yourself with a cloud, so that no prayer can pass through.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have covered yourself with a cloud, so that no prayer can pass through.” Arminian readers see the felt barrier as the consequence of persistent sin (compare Isaiah 59:2), and they note that the community still prays, keeping open the way of return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cloud as God’s withdrawal of felt favor in judgment, which some readers hear as a reversal of the cloud of his presence in the wilderness, and they hold that he still hears his people in his time (compare 3:55–57). Shared ground: both traditions take seriously the experience of prayer that seems blocked.

verses.text: You have made us an off-scouring and refuse in the middle of the peoples.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have made us an off-scouring and refuse in the middle of the peoples.” Arminian readers hear the shame of a people once called to show the LORD’s ways among the nations, now despised among them, and they see this as the bitter result of covenant unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the humiliation as God’s judgment on his people before the nations, a judgment that does not cancel his purposes for them (compare 1 Corinthians 4:13, where Paul uses similar language of the apostles). Shared ground: both traditions read the line as an honest cry of shame brought before God.

verses.text: “All our enemies have opened their mouth wide against us.
verses.arminianNotes: “All our enemies have opened their mouth wide against us” (compare 2:16, where nearly the same words appear). Arminian readers note that enemy scorn adds to the community’s pain, and they see the people bringing even this mockery before God rather than answering it themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the mocking enemies as instruments God has used in judgment, who remain accountable for their contempt (compare 3:64–66). Shared ground: both traditions read the line as lament over enemy derision, and both note that it prepares for the later plea for justice.

verses.text: Terror and the pit have come on us, devastation and destruction.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Terror and the pit have come on us, devastation and destruction” closes the community’s prayer. Arminian readers hear a summary of the catastrophe and see the confession left unresolved, which honors the reality of grief before the afflicted man’s voice returns in 3:48.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the terror and the pit as covenant curse fulfilled (compare Isaiah 24:17; Jeremiah 48:43, which join terror or fear with the pit and the snare), yet still within God’s rule. Shared ground: both traditions let the prayer end as it does, without resolving it early, and receive it as Scripture’s honest speech in disaster.
